speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion in a case of urgent and pressing necessity. The urgency of this matter is recognized in the Speech from the Throne, which declares that the first objective of the government in dealing with inflation will include measures to increase food production, and to this end will provide incentives to our fishermen and ensure that Canada has a right to manage its coastal resources and conserve our fish stocks. That this House, noting the failure of the recent Law of the Sea Conference to recognize and confirm Canada's right to protect and preserve its fisheries resources against reckless over-fishing by foreign nations, urges the government to take immediate steps by unilateral action to conserve our fish stocks, and thereby enable our fishermen to increase production and to assist the government in its fight against inflation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs, but first I should like to congratulate him on his appointment to his new post.
My question comes close to home. In view of the destruction caused by the Russian fishing fleet on July 11, 1974 to the deep sea lobster traps which are valued by their owner, McLeod Fisheries Limited, in excess of $170,000, what steps have been taken by the Canadian government to secure compensation from the Russians for these and other staggering losses? Also, what steps, if any, have been taken to prevent a recurrence of these losses which are destroying the livelihood of our east coast fishermen and fishing companies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

subsubtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. LOUIS DUCLOS AND SECONDED BY MR. ART LEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be words of thanks addressed to the right hon. Prime Minister and the members of the cabinet for having entrusted me with the pleasant task of moving the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Not only is it a mark of confidence which I appreciate greatly, but it is as well an honour of which I am very proud and which is shared by my family and the population of my

October 1, 1974
The Address-Mr. Duclos
riding of Montmorency which was kind enough to trust me in the last general election.
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to congratulate you on the important task that has been entrusted to you. I wish you every success and satisfaction in the performance of your duties as Speaker of this House.
In another vein, I am sorry the absence of our Governor General has cast a shadow over the opening session of this 30th Parliament. I am sure that I speak for all hon. members in this House in wishing him prompt recovery and return to the performance of his high duties. It is however reassuring, Mr. Speaker, to see that he is replaced, in the circumstances, by a person of the calibre of the Right Hon. Justice Bora Laskin.
Mr. Speaker, as is the tradition, I would like to begin by saying some words about the riding I have the privilege of representing since the election of last July. The constituency of Montmorency was created for the election of 1965. Located northeast of Quebec City, it stretches from the towns of Charlesbourg and Orsainville, directly north of Quebec City, whose northeastern limits it follows, then along the St. Lawrence River, down to the town of Saint-Joachim, located some 30 miles east of Quebec City. In short, there are approximately 21 towns and cities in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, most members would better understand if I told them that in the constituency of Montmorency we find this natural jewel that is tie d'Orleans, also Montmorency Falls, the well-known sanctuary of Sainte Anne de Beaupre as well as Mont Sainte Anne ski centre.
A large part of the riding of Montmorency covers what used to be an agricultural area, the lie d'Orleans on the one hand and the stretch of land bordering the St. Lawrence between Ange-Gardien and the municipality of Saint-Joachim, on the other hand.
It is said that today hardly 2 per cent of the labour force in the riding of Montmorency are working in agriculture. Indeed, most of the people are employed in the manufacturing and construction industries, in government and related services, in business and the public service in general.
An integral part of the greater Quebec City area, the riding of Montmorency experiences a progress that is closely dependent on and related to the development of the area as a whole. Some of the investments the federal government contributed these last few years to the substructure in the greater Quebec City area directly benefit-ted the population of the riding of Montmorency. I would like to list a few of these investments. For instance, there is the $18 million granted for the construction of Capital Boulevard, the circular road around Greater Quebec City which allows the people of the Montmorency constituency to gain quick access to the western part of the Quebec City area. There are also the facilities at Mont Sainte-Anne to which the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has earmarked $13 million. Finally, there is the widening of Henri-Bourassa Boulevard, for which the Department has spent $9 million to link Capital Boulevard to the sand banks of Beauport so that, eventually, and as soon as possible, they may be converted into a port.

I have mentioned all these investments, Mr. Speaker, but, in my opinion, they must be only a beginning. Indeed, the economic development needs of my constituency are great, especially since it has an unemployment rate of approximately 8 per cent. It is therefore important that policies be implemented to create in Greater Quebec City a centre of economic development which will allow it to back up the area of Montreal, which now contains the whole Quebec manufacturing industry. In my opinion, any strategy aiming at creating such a development centre must be based upon the development of the port of Quebec City. But, as shown in a report prepared for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, it would be only natural for the port of Quebec City, where activity has more than doubled during the last five years, to be expanded eastwards, in other words, towards the Montmorency constituency. This would mean a gradual conversion of the sand banks, that is, of the part of the constituency which includes the land between the properties of the Anglo Canadian Pulp and Paper Mills Limited and the bridge of Orleans Island.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, several factors would make such a government initiative desirable. First, the fact that the channel to the south of Orleans Island is now being dredged to a depth of 41 feet, which would allow access to 125,000-tonners, ships with a 54-foot draught. For example, because of the river's configuration, only ships of 40,000 tons can reach the Montreal harbour.
One must also take into account the quantity of space available; there is a five mile long zone, which is about 500 feet deep, that could be used for a port.
There is also additional space available behind port facilities that could be used for an industrial harbour sector.
Finally, the sandbanks are linked by the Henri-Bourassa boulevard I just mentioned and boulevard de la Capitale with the main roads of the Quebec and Canada network.
Such a development of the port of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, would undoubtedly attract advanced technology industries that would create well paid jobs for this group of technologists and skilled workers formed of many young people entering the labour market.
Those industries can pay attractive wages more especially owing to their extremely high productivity rate.
I also wish to point out the importance of a direct air service between New York and Quebec City. Such a connection would promote the development of tourism which is centered in my constituency on the sports activities at Mont Sainte-Anne. Indeed, it would give rise to a greater influx of American tourists who would come to ski during winter. I therefore hope that the government will take the necessary steps in order that the difficult negotiations undertaken with the American government be successfully completed.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned a while ago that the Orleans Island appeared to me to be a natural gem. For this reason, I would like to express my appreciation to the federal government for its financial contribution for carrying out a protection and development plan of the Orleans Island.
It seems essential to me that we avoid that economic development, without being against it, should be tan-
October 1, 1974

tamount to the destruction of this peaceful green oasis. The agricultural character of the Island of Orleans must also be protected.
Concerning this, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stress the government's interest, as it was set out in the Speech from the Throne, in encouraging farmers-because, on the Island of Orleans, there are still many farms-to increase their production thanks to policies concerning the stabilization of income and markets.
I am therefore inviting all hon. members to come visit the Montmorency constituency to know it better. They will soon see that the people are hospitable and that it is a good place to live.
I would, however, like to address this invitation more particularly to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I can assure him that the population of Montmorency will make him forget the comportment of the loudmouths that he met in the Quebec region at the opening of the "Superfrancofete", and who tried to violate his rights of liberty of expression in our democratic country. The great majority of the population of Montmorency disapproves of such actions and I wanted to tell this to the Prime Minister in the House.
Mr. Speaker, Paul Valery has said: If the state is too strong, it crushes us; if it is weak, we perish.
In 1967, he who is now head of the Canadian government today, wrote, on somewhat the same lines:
The oldest problem in political philosophy and almost its only one, is to justify authority without, for that, destroying the human person's independence. How can we reconcile the individual and society? The wish to be alone and the need to live in a group? The love of liberty and the necessity for order? ... Now, the most useful thing that philosophy has been able to tell us concerning this problem is that one must stay at equal distance from both ends of the alternative. Too much authority, or too little, and that is the end of liberty.
This is the political philosophy on which are based all the legislative measures which the government intends to take within the next few months to ensure Canada's social and economic progress in these difficult times, measures which are fully described in the Speech from the Throne. No doubt the present situation demands a positive and strong action on the part of the government, but an action which nevertheless shows respect for the individual and his initiative.
Mr. Speaker, the problem of inflation will indeed be at the focus of the government's preoccupations within the next few months. Nearly everybody will agree that, if we want to attack the root of inflation, this is a problem whose solution must be of world wide dimension.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, one must welcome the intention of the government, as outlined in the Speech from the Throne, to participate actively in bilateral and multilateral discussions with a view to ensuring that the present economic difficulties of the world be gradually ironed out and a recession avoided. Under the present circumstances, the state of the world's economy must be the main field of interest of our foreign policy.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is in a position to play a decisive and vital role in bringing together
The Address-Mr. Duclos
the nations of the world in view of the enormous prestige, respect and moral authority enjoyed by its Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the international arena. As of now, all our efforts must be geared toward bringing as many countries as possible to a better understanding of the urgency of genuine international co-operation in the field of monetary and trade policies.
The Speech from the Throne also refers to the government's concern with respect to the spreading of nuclear technology and materials. This is, in my view, a problem of utmost importance in view of the always increasing number of countries which have developed, or appear on the verge of developing, nuclear capability. I would hope that Conrad Adenauer, the late father of West Germany, was mistaken when he said: "God made a great mistake when he limited the intelligence of man but did not limit his stupidity". The American novelist, John Steinbeck, once wrote on the same subject: "Our civil war has been called the last of the gentlemen's wars". The so-called Second World War was surely the last of the long, global wars. The next war, if we are so stupid as to let it happen, will be the last of any kind; there will be no one left to remember anything-and if that is how stupid we are, we do not, in a biological sense, deserve survival.

Mr. Speaker, as regards the inflation problem I mentioned a while ago, one may be sure that if international concertation is necessary to really tackle this problem, we should not for all that minimize the importance of the measures proposed by the government, measures that follow those taken in the past and which permitted Canada, in the circumstances, to show a lower price increase rate than that shown in other industrialized countries.
Mr. Speaker, therefore I should like to suggest a serious examination of the part played by credit cards in the inflation problem. Indeed, one can wonder if their extensive use nowadays could not destroy the measures that the government might put into effect to restrict the demand for goods and services.
Housing is another sector of our economy where inflation is causing havoc. All were able to notice the abnormal rise in housing during these last years, especially in the great urban centres of this country. There are obviously various causes, but it seems to me that we should examine the part played by land speculation and, if need be, the possibility of introducing a special tax on profits derived from speculative transactions.
Mr. Speaker, it is all the more necessary for our economy to keep and increase its strength since that is the essential condition to the improvement of our social security program. For it is basically the increase in the strength of our economy that will allow this government to be even more generous in the case of the small and the underprivileged in our society. I always thought, Mr. Speaker, that the role of the government in a country as affluent as Canada is basically to be with the small, the underprivileged, and to stand for them.
I am also pleased to note in the Speech from the Throne the government project with respect to allowances for the

October 1, 1974
The Address-Mr. Duclos
spouses of old age security recipients between the ages of 60 and 65. I hope this will be a first step toward the eventual payment of old age security to those reaching 60 and wishing to withdraw from the labour force. Of course, one must be fully aware of the costs inherent in such social legislation but it will be through the expansion of our economy that we will be able to help the truly needy.
The Speech from the Throne is also quite comforting as far as housing goes, particularly as it relates to making it easier for young people to buy a first home. I refer particularly to the $500 grant on buying a first home, and in the case of a new house. Finally, I refer to a measure contained in the budget-the housing savings plan-to allow at last young people to prepare through the years for the purchase of a home. I also point out a proposal quite popular and welcomed in my riding. I am talking about the federal rebate which allows the government and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to reimburse part of the monthly mortgage payments actually beyond what Canadian families can afford to pay.
Those proposals are quite welcomed in my riding where there is a large proportion of young households anxious to settle down in their own homes after a few years of married life.
Mr. Speaker, at the opening of the first session of the 29th Parliament, the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker) who seconded the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, stated:
There are those who claim that the bilingualization of the public service has gone too far too fast. May I say with great respect to the members of this House that it has proceeded not too quickly, but altogether too slowly.
I would like to tell, Mr. Speaker, how much these comments seemed right to me then. I know that there is constant progress in that field but I also know that there is still much to be done.
However, being forever concerned about the rights of the people in office the government must nevertheless increase its efforts so that French-speaking Canadians may carve out a career in the Public Service of Canada while keeping their culture. It is imperative that the experts trained by Quebec at the cost of huge sacrifices on the part of the Quebec population find outlets in the Public Service of Canada and contribute to increase further its quality.
It is regrettable that due to the nationalist wave which has invaded many Quebec sectors too many young French Quebecers give up in such a way quite interesting careers and deprive society of valuable services.
Mr. Speaker, to conclude, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee), that an Address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada, the text of which is as follows:
To His Excellency the Right Hon. Bora Laskin, Chief Justice of Canada and Administrator of the Government of Canada.
May it please Your Excellency:
We, Her Majesty's most loyal and dutiful subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency

for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both Houses of Parliament.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS IN REPLY, MOVED BY MR. LOUIS DUCLOS AND SECONDED BY MR. ART LEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege for me to be accorded this opportunity to second the motion of the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos). It is an honour for the people of my constituency of Vancouver East and a recognition of my province and the west.
I am deeply appreciative that I have been chosen to represent one of the most interesting and challenging constituencies in Canada, an area made up of hard working and talented people many of whom have come from other countries to make this their home. There are thousands of native born as well, and together we represent a great range of ethnic backgrounds and many political parties. We have Canadians who have come from Italy, Germany, Yugoslavia, The Netherlands, from other European and Asiatic countries and, of course, from Great Britain. We are glad they chose Canada, and I shall represent them with pride.
Then there are the Canadians of Chinese descent. If you will forgive a personal note, Mr. Speaker and hon. members, my election to parliament as the first Canadian of Chinese descent from my party tells something about this great country of Canada. My family had its beginning in Canada when my great grandfather came here in 1883 to work on the Canadian Pacific Railway as a labourer. It may be said that in a very real and tangible way Canadians of Chinese descent helped unite Canada in the first place with bands of steel. My grandfather ran a grocery store and restaurant in the Cranbrook and Kimberley area from 1902 to 1937. His son, my father, continued my grandfather's business until World War II, when he served as a pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force. My father later co-founded an independent retailer-owned wholesale business in Edmonton, Alberta, which services northern Alberta, the Northwest Territories and the Arctic.
Within four generations this great country of ours has provided the chance for our family-yes, and to many other families of many other backgrounds-to build our lives and careers and to take advantage of the great range of opportunities available to all Canadians.
Of course, together with certain other groups in society, the efforts of Canadians of Chinese descent to achieve the full privileges of citizenship have not been without problems. Many of my ancestors have known hardships born from misunderstanding and language barriers. But, through perseverence and patience and by drawing on their strength and cultural upbringing, they have now achieved full and equal participation in Canadian life. Many of us have entered the professions but, more important, we as an ethnic community have become more actively involved in our society and will continue to do so.
I stand before you, Mr. Speaker, as a member of a new generation of Canadians and I consider it my task as a member of parliament to represent and serve all the people of my riding of Vancouver East, my province, British Columbia, and my country, Canada. I consider myself privileged to be a member of the post-Second

World War generation. We are fortunate that our grandfathers and fathers defended this nation in two world wars and overcame the very real hardships of the depression years. I think I speak for all young Canadians when I say that we have had opportunities like no one before us. At times, admittedly, some of our actions and expressions would not appear to express this gratitude, but many of our critical attitudes and actions have been inspired by a sincere desire to better what we believe to be basically a good society. I am young in years, but my cultural heritage has taught me to draw on the wisdom that comes with age. I look forward to drawing upon the wisdom of my new colleagues be they on this side or the other side of the aisle.
My great constituency, Vancouver East, is an urban riding. The eastern half of the port of Vancouver is its northern boundary. Another notable landmark, the Pacific National Exhibition-the largest exhibition on the west coast and the second largest in Canada-is held yearly in Vancouver East. Vancouver city hall and the Vancouver General hospital are situated in my riding. The second largest Italian community in Canada is also in Vancouver East. Because of these special attributes and, if I may say this in all modesty, Mr. Speaker, because my riding is in Vancouver, one of the most beautiful cities in the whole of Canada, I believe I have been afforded the opportunity to serve and represent the most interesting and unique riding in the country.
Because Vancouver East has been, and still is, the staging ground for many new Canadians, the general question of assimilation is of special concern and importance to many of the people I represent. I trust that the measures outlined in the throne speech will give some of the answers to this question. Housing in general is also of great concern to the people of Vancouver East. I welcome the measures outlined in the Speech from the Throne. Hopefully, they will assist greatly in alleviating the need for improving accommodations.
Furthermore, my riding, being an integral part of the greater Vancouver area, is faced with the problems of an urban environment. The quality of the environment in physical, economic and social terms is of great concern to the people of Vancouver East. I trust the measures outlined in the throne speech will help to alleviate this problem of urbanization.
Many senior citizens live in my riding. My cultural heritage has taught me to respect my elders and to be responsible for them. In exercising our responsibility for our senior citizens, we should do so with dignity and honour; not out of a sense of charity but because our senior citizens have earned it.
Of great concern to the people of Vancouver East is the state of the nation's economy, particularly in these times of inflation. I have the fullest confidence that the measures outlined in the Speech from the Throne will help to control and curb the problem of inflation. Most gratifying is the policy that inflation shall not be combated by the government's deliberately causing slack in the economy.
The Address-Mr. Lee
Mr. Speaker, because of my family's roots and because I represent British Columbia, one of the western provinces,
I feel that I should speak briefly as a westerner. It is true that Canada is made up of many diversified regions and economies. It is equally true that western Canada in its make-up is not homogeneous but is, in reality, very heterogeneous. There are, however, some regional traits common to British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. First, industries in western Canada are predominately resource-oriented. Second, westerners are individualists; each of us has a feeling that we can make our own way and direct our own life. Third, westerners judge a person for what he or she is, and not so much on the basis of where he or sheeomes from. Fourth, westerners take great pride in our earnest hopes for a unified Canada based on the diversity of our ethnic origins. Because of these regional traits, we feel that the west is unique and we earnestly hope that this thirtieth parliament, as have parliaments in the past, will give more recognition to the problems of the west.
We are gratified to see that the throne speech for this session is working toward a long-term program in transportation. Our concern is based upon the fact that western Canada's economic position depends heavily on transportation, and any attempt to strengthen western economy will necessarily involve improvements to the transportation system. In addition to our concern over transportation, we earnestly hope that more recognition will be given to the fact that western Canada needs to develop a viable secondary industry. To accomplish this goal there is further need for more decentralization of industrial activity in the west, both in the private and government sectors.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned earlier that the northern boundary of my riding is the eastern half of the port of Vancouver. Being also an integral part of the west's economic structure, we earnestly hope that more recognition will be given to that port's need for future development. Our concern is based upon the fact that unless further recognition is forthcoming, the hopes and aspirations that western Canada, and Canada in general, will become an integral part of the Pacific rim will be frustrated.
I should like at this time to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for giving me the opportunity to second the motion of the hon. member for Montmorency. I should also like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members present, for your courteous patience with a freshman member of parliament. I take pleasure in seconding the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
